entries.title: Over 1,000 birds hurt, killed after hitting Chicago buildings over weekend
entries.summary: <p>As millions of migratory birds passed through Chicago over the weekend, at least 1,000 of them ended up dead and injured after colliding into buildings. </p><p>The fall bird migration hits its peak in October, and Chicago sits along one of North America's biggest migratory paths. And thanks to favorable weather over the weekend, over five million migratory birds <a class="Link" href="https://dashboard.birdcast.org/region/US-IL-031?night=2026-10-16" target="_blank" >passed through Cook County</a> Friday night alone. </p><p>About 25 volunteers with the Chicago Bird Collision Monitors were out Saturday collecting dead and injured birds, said Annette Prince, the organization's director. </p><p>"We were out from 6 a.m. to sunset," Prince said. "We'd pick up a bird at a building, go around that building, and immediately find another. We had birds hitting the glass windows over our heads." </p><p>Her group has a hotline people can call if they've found an injured bird. At one point on Saturday, the phone was ringing every 30 seconds, Prince said. </p><p>"It was overwhelming, but also very rewarding that people are noticing this and reaching out," Prince said. </p><p>Volunteers collected over 1,000 birds. Dead birds are brought to the Field Museum for research. Injured birds were taken for treatment at the DuPage Wildlife Conservation Center, which reported <a class="Link" href="https://www.facebook.com/dupagewildlifeconservationcenter" target="_blank" >receiving over 250 birds</a> on Saturday. </p><p>While that number sounds high, those are just the ones that volunteers found. It's likely many more birds were injured or killed over the weekend, Prince said. </p><p>"It was shocking and heartbreaking to see how it can add up," Prince said. "These birds deserve our protection. ... The least we can do is give them safe passage through our area." </p><p>The weekend's toll was a reminder that there's much more Chicago can do to protect migratory birds, Prince said. Currently, developers can voluntarily choose to outfit their new buildings with bird-safe features. </p><p>One of those features is to install textured glass that birds are able to see as a solid structure. After over <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/10/6/23906778/birds-killed-migration-collision-mccormick-place-lakeside-center" target="_blank" >1,000 birds hit</a> McCormick Place Lakeside Center in a single night three years ago, bird-safe film was installed on the building's windows. Collisions <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2025/01/08/bird-collisions-down-mccormick-place-environment" target="_blank" >dramatically dropped</a> as a result. </p><p>Prince and other advocates are pushing the Chicago City Council to <a class="Link" href="https://chicityclerkelms.chicago.gov/Matter/?matterId=45E30885-F122-F111-8341-001DD80C2AAC" target="_blank" >pass an ordinance</a> requiring certain new buildings or major renovations in Chicago to include bird-friendly protections. Similar laws have been passed in New York City, San Francisco and Washington, D.C., Prince said. </p><p>"Development hasn't stopped in those cities, it's not stopped architects from making beautiful buildings," Prince said. "Chicago can have beautiful buildings and beautiful birds, and they can all coexist. ... We can't afford to lose birds that are already struggling to survive."</p>

entries.title: Early voting kicks off in all 50 wards
entries.summary: <p>Richard Rolark wanted to avoid the lines, the hassle and the possibility of bad weather on Election Day in two weeks.</p><p>“It’s a good convenience for older people, especially here on the South Side. And on Nov. 3, you don’t know what the weather is going to be like. This is Chicago, after all. We might have eight inches of snow and 40 degrees below zero,” Rolark, 76. said Monday morning outside the 4th Ward voting site at the Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Center.</p><p>Expanded in-person early voting for the Nov. 3 general election <a class="Link" href="https://chicagoelections.gov/news/expanded-person-early-voting-opens-today-all-50-chicago-wards-november-3rd-general-election" target="_blank" >started Monday in all 50 Chicago wards</a> and at three Chicago-area universities.</p><p>In the city, voters are choosing the president and members of the Chicago Board of Education. Statewide, voters are casting ballots in races for the U.S. Senate, the U.S. House of Representatives, Illinois governor and lieutenant governor,, as well as attorney general, other statewide offices entries.title: Pilsen nonprofit a finalist in national affordable housing solutions program
entries.summary: <p>The Resurrection Project, a Pilsen-based nonprofit, was announced as a finalist in Capital One’s $25 million Scaling Pathways to Homeownership initiative that saw 500 applicants from across the country.</p><p>Resurrection and nine other finalists will each receive $200,000, plus technical assistance, to strengthen their proposals on how to tackle the nation's affordable housing crisis, Capital One said in a news release last week. Resurrection was the only Illinois finalist.</p><p>The 10 organizations will have three months to work on their proposals, then five will be selected in spring 2027, with each receiving $4.6 million to bring their solutions to life.</p><p>Capital One launched <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/10/29/capital-one-affordable-housing-chicago-nonprofit-lever-change" >Scaling Pathways to Homeownership</a> in October 2025, in partnership with the Chicago nonprofit Lever for Change. The $25 million program challenged applicants to think of innovative solutions to the country's affordable housing crisis. The banking company suggested housing counseling, consumer education and for-sale housing production at scale as the building blocks for submissions.</p><p>Resurrection’s proposal is to expand its Full Circle Homes initiative statewide. The program now serves residents in the southwest Chicago area and helps them with the homebuying process, from coaching and lending to supportive services that help clients stay in their homes. </p><p>“We know that these barriers are real, and yet we are helping families successfully purchase a home,” Kristen Komara, Resurrection’s vice president of Full Circle Homes, said. “We know that what we're doing already is working, and so we saw this opportunity from Capital One to take our model and what we know helps an individual and families become a successful homeowner and scale that beyond the geographies where we work.”</p><p>Komara said Chicagoans are being inundated with messages that home ownership is out of reach, but their program has helped more than 250 families buy a home in the last year and a half. </p><p>If selected by Capital One, Resurrection would expand Full Circle Homes with the help of partner organizations. It also wants to develop a Full Circle Homes mobile app that would help potential buyers build mortgage readiness skills, among other services.</p><p>“We feel like a big need for the communities that we serve is just having a very engaging, client-friendly, client-facing technology that can walk someone through the entire process of buying a home,” Komara said. “We have a vision for it to be multilingual, so it's reaching populations that we're not able to currently serve. We definitely see this as a way to make our services and our homeownership model more accessible.”</p><p>The Scaling Pathways to Homeownership program is part of Capital One’s $265 billion Community Benefits Plan, which turns "innovative ideas into scalable, real-world solutions for low- and moderate-income communities,” Kerone Vatel, Capital One’s senior vice president and head of community finance, impact and investment, said in a news release. </p><p>The London-based nonprofit consultancy Spring Impact is providing the technical assistance to finalists. </p><p>The other nine finalists are: Community Redevelopment Agency of Jackson in Tennessee; Four Bands Community Fund in South Dakota; Great Lakes Housing Services in Michigan; Habitat for Humanity NYC and Westchester County in New York; Hope Enterprise Corp. in Mississippi; Mountain Shadow Association in Montana; Self-Help Enterprises in California; Southside Community Development and Housing Corp. in Virginia; and St. Louis Community Foundation in Missouri.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/10/17/mortgage-rates-home-prices-sidelining-buyers-purchase-redfin-report" >Rising mortgage rates and home prices sidelining buyers but now is the time to purchase, report says</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/10/29/capital-one-affordable-housing-chicago-nonprofit-lever-change" >Capital One partners with Chicago nonprofit to fund ideas for affordable housing solutions</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: After Atlanta, it's clearer than ever Bears' championship aspirations ride on QB Caleb Williams
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback Caleb Williams was nearly perfect Sunday in his return from a hamstring injury. His decision making, his throws, his poise, his energy — everything the Bears dreamed of when they drafted him showed up in their 31-23 win over the Falcons.</p><p>But, as veteran Case Keenum pointed out following his sparkling game against the Eagles last month, the NFL rewards great performances by immediately demanding them again.</p><p>Williams certainly isn’t expected to duplicate what he did Sunday on a regular basis — completing 30 of his 36 passes was phenomenal — but he is looking to establish consistency somewhere in that neighborhood. That’s what it’ll take to put the Bears in the Super Bowl conversation, and the assignment gets tougher with the Patriots and Seahawks coming up next.</p><p>Those teams played in the Super Bowl last season and are led by two of the NFL’s preeminent defensive coaches in New England’s Mike Vrabel and Seattle’s Mike MacDonald, a pair of masterminds capable of playing chess with Williams and coach Ben Johnson.</p><p>The Patriots are the No. 6 defense in the league and the defending champion Seahawks are No. 1. Both are in the top half of the league in pressuring quarterbacks and overall pass defense.</p><p>Williams faces a quick turnaround with the Patriots coming to Soldier Field on Thursday, then an extended opportunity to regroup before the Bears visit the Seahawks on Nov. 2.</p><p>The short week is tough as it is, but especially challenging for Williams as he deals with ongoing injury maintenance. He said last week that while he was healthy enough to play, he wasn’t fully healed and would need to put in extra time between games to keep himself in playing condition.</p><p>“Lots of treatment,” Williams said Sunday of his plans leading up to the Patriots game. “Studying film while I’m watching treatment. It’s just another thing that’s added to my day. It’s going to be like that for the rest of the year. Just making sure I’m on top of it.</p><p>“After a 60-minute game, I feel pretty good. I have no stiffness, no tightness. ... I’ve got to let the adrenaline settle down and figure out how I feel after that.”</p><p>Sore, probably. It’ll be difficult to come back Thursday with the same electricity, but he and the Bears knew what they were getting into when they brought him back in Atlanta rather than wait for the Patriots game.</p><p>It’s the next step for Williams in a season that already has been all over the place.</p><p>He was fantastic in the Bears’ season-opening win over the Panthers, then struggled significantly against the Vikings the next week before leaving with the hamstring strain.</p><p>All quarterbacks hit rough patches, and Josh Allen and Matthew Stafford are among those who have turned in total duds this season, but each of them has a track record a mile long and can write those games off as aberrations. That’s where Williams wants to be.</p><p>In his return Sunday, he played what Hall of Famer Tom Brady called the best game of his career as he completed 83.3% of his passes, second-highest in team history and threw for 305 yards and a touchdown for a 111.8 passer rating.</p><p>Williams deflected Brady's comment, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/09/01/the-bears-and-their-fans-needed-a-truth-teller-they-got-one-in-new-coach-ben-johnson" >sounding a lot like coach Ben Johnson</a>.</p><p>“When you win, it covers up things,” Williams said. “When you lose, it shows everything. We’ll be truth tellers about ourselves and figure out what we need to fix and get better.”</p><p>That game steadied his season stats at a 72.5 completion percentage, which leads the league, a 101.5 passer rating and an average of 237.3 yards passing per game. Those are reasonable targets for him. If he settles into that level of efficiency and production — or better, of course — all questions will be answered.</p><p>Playing like that also would mean two substantive developments for the Bears: Williams being able to compensate for other personnel deficiencies and giving his team a shot at competing for a championship. Those are high on the list of job requirements for a franchise quarterback.</p><p>One of the most impressive parts of Williams’ game against the Falcons is that he carried the offense, which was missing No. 2 running back Kyle Monangai, when the rushing attack fell flat. D’Andre Swift averaged just 2.8 yards per carry, while Roschon Johnson added 3.9.</p><p>Williams also navigated instability on the offensive line, though he did take four sacks, and spread his passes among eight receivers.</p><p>Those are all signs of a quarterback stepping into his own and not being dependent on his circumstances.</p><p>And coming off a season in which the Bears went 11-6 and came within a couple plays of reaching the NFC Championship Game, they’re aiming for a deeper playoff run. That will hinge, more than anything, on Williams.</p><p>The roster, while imperfect, looks ready enough. The Bears have sufficient pieces on the offensive line when healthy, a talented group of skill players, a top-10 defense and a credible coach.</p><p>From there, everything rides on Williams. Whether he’s good, great or erratic, the Bears will be as well. He played at a championship level Sunday, and more of that would give his team a chance against anybody.</p>

entries.title: Patrick Kane shares his thoughts on Blackhawks' first nine games
entries.summary: <p>Patrick Kane, Connor Bedard and Roman Kantserov came to a realization while watching video clips before <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> practice last Friday.</p><p>"We looked at our rushes and, as a line, we were like, 'Let's get someone to drive the middle of the ice,'" Kane said.</p><p>Added coach Jeff Blashill: "It’s hard to get some of the seam passes to open up because you don’t have that middle drive."</p><p>As they crossed the red line during a third-period rush <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/10/17/blackhawks-stars-connor-bedard-spencer-knight" >Saturday</a>, they successfully put that plan into action. Kantserov turned on his jets and pushed back Stars defenseman Nils Lundkvist with a center-lane drive, allowing Bedard — skating with the puck down the right wing — to find Kane wide-open with a perfect pass.</p><p>That's a great example of the value of ample video review and practice time for the 3-6-0 Hawks, who are not only young but also don't have a ton of familiarity with each other yet.</p><p>Since Monday marked the first of three consecutive practices before their next game Friday, this week offers a prime opportunity for more breakthroughs.</p><p>Knowing that, Kane, Bedard and Kantserov all hit the ice early to work on further refining their rush strategies.</p><p>"Now it's like, 'OK, how can we do that and get the puck carrier to the middle of the ice if there's space?'" Kane said. </p><p>"When you watch guys around the league, sometimes it's just as simple as your first touch on a puck, bringing it to the middle of the ice. That sets you up for space instead of taking it wide, [because] maybe then you get squeezed off."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">What a pass from Bedard but Kane puts it wide: <a href="https://t.co/z5GEflOmCr">pic.twitter.com/z5GEflOmCr</a></p>— BHF (@BlackhawksFocus) <a href="https://x.com/BlackhawksFocus/status/2111630683663688139?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">October 18, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Kane is also personally using this week to think about how to bear down on chances. Through nine games, the 37-year-old future Hall of Famer is stuck on one goal — which he scored all the way back in the opener — and four assists.</p><p>During his five-on-five ice time, he has only two points, and the Hawks have been outscored 11-2 and outshot 75-47.</p><p>Only three of those games have been <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/10/16/blackhawks-connor-bedard-first-games-back" >with Bedard</a>, and he and Kane have shown promise together, even though the analytics don't yet reflect it.</p><p>But Kane is responsible for his own finishing, and he hasn't been satisfied with that. He was especially upset about missing the net on that aforementioned third-period chance Saturday.</p><p>"The production and numbers aren't there, so obviously that's disappointing," Kane said. "It's not a dream start for me. But I still think there's moments throughout the game where there's times you could create. [The] numbers could be a little bit different.</p><p>"Even last game, you're coming out of the rink pissed off, and then you watch it over and it's like, 'There's some moments there where the game could've changed and you could've been on the scoresheet.' [Like when] Roman's in front, he has an open net and [his shot] hits [Lundkvist's] leg and the post."</p><p>Leadership-wise, Kane has spent recent weeks reminding his younger teammates that "everyone's in here for a reason," encouraging them to remain confident in their unique skills and playing styles.</p><p>He mentioned several examples Monday of that paying off: Bedard "coming back and playing well," Kantserov scoring twice last Tuesday, Artyom Levshunov scoring in overtime last Thursday, Frank Nazar "flying" and Anton Frondell looking "like he's going to be a big-time player."</p><p>Kane believes the Hawks' lingering problems stem more from mistakes or poor execution of systems than from flaws in the roster. And those could be reduced by simply finding ways to "take the risk out of our game."</p><p>"I don't think it's a talent issue at all, to be honest," he added. "It's just the way we're playing. </p><p>"You see a lot of mistakes either come when we have the puck on our sticks or give up odd-man rushes when there's no need to."</p>

entries.title: Chicago aprueba $260.8 millones para 17 víctimas de abuso policial a manos del exoficial corrupto Reynaldo Guevara
entries.summary: <p>El Concejo Municipal acordó el miércoles pagar un acuerdo global de $260.8 millones a 17 demandantes a quienes el corrupto exdetective de la Policía de Chicago, Reynaldo Guevara, les inventó casos de asesinato, esto en un esfuerzo por evitar veredictos “desbocados” de jurados que, advirtió un abogado de la Ciudad, podrían haber superado los $1,000 millones.</p><p>Tan amarga como sea la píldora para los contribuyentes de Chicago, el riesgo de ir a juicio con jurado habría sido mayor.</p><p>La subjefa del asesor jurídico corporativo, Jessica Felker, advirtió al Comité de Finanzas que los jurados son impredecibles y que a tres demandantes, en los últimos años, les otorgaron $170 millones por 42 años de prisión, lo que equivale a más de $4 millones por año.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-310000" name="module-310000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>El acuerdo aprobado el miércoles resolverá 16 demandas por mala conducta policial y equivale a casi $680,000 por cada uno de los casi 384 años que los 17 beneficiarios pasaron colectivamente en prisión.</p><p>Las 17 condenas por asesinato —relacionadas con hechos que se remontan incluso a 1987— fueron luego anuladas. Al momento de ser arrestados por asesinato, los demandantes tenían entre 14 y 28 años. En promedio, pasaron 22.6 años en prisión cada uno.</p><p>Cuarenta y tres personas, incluidas tres mujeres, han sido exoneradas después de ser enviadas a prisión por condenas por asesinato en casos manejados por Guevara en las décadas de 1980 y 1990. La mayoría vivía en Humboldt Park.</p><p>El acuerdo en los casos de Guevara se pagará en dos años, a partir de 2027, en cuatro cuotas de $65 millones cada una.</p><p>Casi triplica el <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/10/02/victims-90-million-dollars-police-misconduct-settlement-chicago-police-ronald-watts" target="_blank" >acuerdo global de $90 millones</a> que puso fin a 176 demandas vinculadas al exsargento de la Policía de Chicago, Ronald Watts, acusado de fabricar casos contra cientos de personas por cargos de drogas en el complejo Ida B. Wells de la Autoridad de Vivienda de Chicago (CHA).</p><p>Desde el acuerdo de Watts, el Concejo Municipal ha presionado a la administración de Johnson para concretar un acuerdo global similar que resuelva decenas de casos de Guevara que aún siguen pendientes.</p><p>Pero el pago aprobado el miércoles y “otros dos en la fila”, como lo expresó Felker, resolverán solo la mitad de los casos pendientes de Guevara. Los otros 23 casos casi con certeza requerirán un acuerdo igualmente grande.</p><p>Hasta ahora, el escándalo de Guevara es, por mucho, el más costoso en la historia del CPD. Supera los $210 millones en acuerdos, sentencias, honorarios legales y reparaciones derivados de los casos de tortura vinculados al excomandante de la Zona 2, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2018/9/19/18476626/former-chicago-police-cmdr-jon-burge-tied-to-torture-cases-has-died" target="_blank" >Jon Burge</a>, y su grupo de cómplices.</p><p>La asesora jurídica corporativa saliente, Mary Richardson-Lowry, sacó adelante el acuerdo de Guevara al despedirse del cargo, y fue elogiada por haberlo logrado.</p><p>El concejal Bill Conway (34.°), exfiscal del Condado Cook, calificó el acuerdo de Guevara como un “acuerdo gigantesco, pero responsable”.</p><p>El concejal Ray Lopez (15.°) también aceptó apoyar el acuerdo “repulsivo, pero necesario”, aunque dijo que no tenía idea “si realmente tenemos el dinero para pagarlo”.</p><p>La concejal Jeanette Taylor (20.°) había expresado antes su frustración por el hecho de que Guevara, quien se retiró del Departamento de Policía de Chicago en junio de 2005, siguiera cobrando una pensión por los 30 años que trabajó en el CPD.</p><p>Felker le dijo a Taylor que una condena por delito grave dentro del ámbito del empleo es la única base para negar una pensión policial, y que Guevara nunca ha sido acusado de un delito.</p><p>Después de la reunión, el alcalde Brandon Johnson dijo a los reporteros que, si es reelegido, exploraría la posibilidad de impulsar cambios en la ley estatal para negarle a Guevara la pensión policial que sigue recibiendo.</p><p>Tras recibir críticas el año pasado por financiar el acuerdo de $90 millones con un préstamo de cinco años, Felker aseguró al Comité de Finanzas que no se recurrirá a ningún endeudamiento para cubrir los $260.8 millones necesarios para pagar a los demandantes de Guevara. Sin embargo, la presidenta del Comité de Finanzas, Pat Dowell, dijo a los reporteros que la administración de Johnson sí tiene previsto pedir dinero prestado para cubrir el acuerdo de Guevara.</p><p>Johnson dijo que no estaba seguro de cómo se pagaría el acuerdo y que está “contento de tener una conversación más detallada” al respecto, presumiblemente después de presentar su presupuesto de 2026 el próximo miércoles.</p><p>También dijo que los contribuyentes “nunca podrán deshacer el daño” causado a los 17 demandantes ni “devolverles lo que perdieron”. Pero añadió que el acuerdo es un paso crucial para “enfrentar las injusticias del pasado”.</p><p>El alcalde también dijo que le anima un nuevo informe que muestra que el Departamento de Policía de Chicago alcanzó un cumplimiento preliminar del 99% del decreto federal de consentimiento que define los términos de la supervisión de las cortes y un cumplimiento total del 32%.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>
